prompt_free_text:
This paper addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between standard motion forecasting benchmarks and real deployment: forecasting in autonomous driving is performed repeatedly over time, yet most benchmark methods treat each scene independently. The paper proposes RealMotion, which augments a standard encoder-decoder predictor with two temporal mechanisms across successive sub-scenes: a scene context stream that propagates scene-level context, and an agent trajectory stream that relays/refines predictions using a trajectory memory bank. The paper also introduces a data reorganization procedure that converts benchmark scenes into short continuous sequences by splitting trajectories at multiple historical timestamps. Empirically, the method reports strong results on Argoverse 2 single-agent and multi-agent leaderboards, competitive results on Argoverse 1, and a favorable efficiency profile.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially impactful. The central premise is compelling: continuous forecasting should exploit temporal continuity across repeated inference calls, and current benchmark protocols indeed obscure this opportunity. The paper also has a practical flavor that is refreshing, especially the explicit distinction between “offline” benchmark evaluation and “online” deployment latency. The reported gains over the independent variant are substantial, and the ablations suggest that both temporal streams contribute. If the empirical claims are robust, this could be a meaningful step toward more realistic forecasting systems.

That said, I also have several concerns about clarity, experimental fairness, and the exact source of the gains. My main reservation is that the paper mixes three contributions that are difficult to disentangle cleanly: a new problem framing, a benchmark/data transformation, and a new model. The strongest empirical improvements appear when all three are combined, but it remains somewhat unclear whether the gains primarily come from the architectural ideas or from training/evaluating on a reorganized setting that may provide additional effective supervision or altered sample statistics. The paper does include an “independent” variant and some ablations, which is helpful, but I do not think the current evidence fully isolates the benefit of continuous temporal reasoning from the benefit of simply exposing the model to more overlapping sub-scenes.

The data reorganization strategy is the most novel aspect from a benchmarking perspective, but also the most delicate one. The paper says each original scene is retrospectively split into multiple sub-scenes using historical split points, with local maps and neighboring agents aggregated at each split point. This is intuitive, but the exact protocol needs to be much more precise for reproducibility and for assessing fairness. For example, how are train/val/test samples constructed from original scenes? Are multiple sub-scenes from the same original scene present in both training and validation/test contexts in a way that could inflate performance through overlap? At test time, is the model evaluated only on the final sub-scene while being allowed to consume earlier sub-scenes from the same original benchmark sample? If so, this is a different evaluation protocol than standard one-shot forecasting, and the comparison to prior leaderboard methods becomes less apples-to-apples unless those methods are also adapted to the same continuous input stream. The paper acknowledges this partially via the “offline” versus “online” distinction, but the fairness issue remains central.

Relatedly, the comparison in Table 1 is potentially misleading unless carefully qualified. RealMotion is compared directly against methods that were trained and evaluated under the standard independent-scene protocol, whereas RealMotion appears to exploit additional sequential context derived from the same original sample. Even if this context would be available in deployment, it is not available to the baselines as reported on the leaderboard. Therefore, the claim of state of the art should be phrased more carefully: it may be state of the art under a continuous-driving reformulation, but not necessarily under the original benchmark setting. The inclusion of RealMotion-I helps, but it is not enough to establish that the architectural innovations alone outperform prior methods under matched inputs. The appendix mention that QCNet can also benefit from the reorganized data structure is promising, but this should be in the main paper with quantitative results. A particularly important baseline would be: take a strong existing model such as QCNet or Forecast-MAE, train it on the reorganized continuous sub-scenes, and optionally feed previous sub-scenes in a simple way. Without such baselines, it is hard to know whether the gains are due to the proposed streams or simply due to the richer training/evaluation setup.

On the modeling side, the scene context stream is reasonable but somewhat incremental. It aligns previous scene features to the current frame using motion-aware layer normalization and then applies cross-attention from current map to previous map and from current agents to previous scene. This is sensible, though the design choices are not deeply justified. Why should map features only attend to historical map features, while agent features attend to the full historical scene? Why is a single previous step sufficient, rather than a longer temporal window or recurrent state compression? The paper says the stream progressively accumulates context, but the exact recurrence is not formalized clearly enough. Is the propagated state simply the updated scene feature from the previous sub-scene, or is there any gating/memory control? Since repeated cross-attention over accumulated features can drift or overfit to stale context, some discussion of stability would be useful.

The agent trajectory stream is more distinctive. Using past predictions as a memory bank to refine current predictions is an appealing idea, especially because repeated forecasting in deployment naturally produces such predictions. However, the current presentation leaves several technical ambiguities. The memory bank stores predicted trajectories and mode features for each agent of interest, but in multi-agent settings it is unclear how identities are maintained across sub-scenes. Does the method assume perfect agent association from the dataset? In real deployment, this would depend on tracking quality. Also, the refinement mechanism uses similarity between current predicted trajectories and aligned historical predicted trajectories via trajectory embeddings. This raises a concern about self-reinforcement: if earlier predictions are wrong, the memory bank may bias later predictions toward those errors. The qualitative examples suggest refinement helps, but I would like to see a failure analysis or at least an ablation on memory bank length and on using ground-truth past futures during training versus predicted ones. Exposure bias seems especially relevant here.

Another concern is whether the method uses information that is unrealistically favorable in the reorganized benchmark. Because the original benchmark scenes already contain a fixed historical window and future horizon, splitting them retrospectively may create sub-scenes whose “past” and “future” are sampled from a single curated clip with complete annotations and no perception uncertainty. This is acceptable for a first study, but it should be discussed more explicitly as a simulation of continuous driving rather than a true streaming benchmark. The paper contrasts itself with Pang et al. on streaming motion forecasting from tracking data, but does not convincingly explain why the proposed transformed benchmark is preferable beyond convenience. In fact, a stronger paper would compare directly against a true streaming benchmark or at least evaluate robustness to missing agents, occlusions, or tracking noise.

The empirical section is strong in breadth but weaker in rigor than it first appears. The leaderboard results are impressive, especially the gains in minFDE1 and minADE1 on Argoverse 2 and the multi-agent improvements. The ablations are useful and generally support the contribution of each component. The efficiency analysis is also appreciated, and the distinction between online and offline latency is important. However, several key experiments are missing. First, there is no direct comparison against temporal baselines adapted to the same continuous setting. Second, there is no statistical analysis or variance across runs; given that some ablation gains are modest, this matters. Third, there is no breakdown by scenario type, such as intersections, lane changes, occlusions, or dense interactions, despite the motivation emphasizing complex temporal context and invisible agents. Such analysis would greatly strengthen the claim that the method helps specifically in situations where continuity matters. Fourth, the paper should report how performance changes as the amount of prior context increases, beyond just split points and gradient steps. For example, does the method continue improving with longer histories, or saturate quickly?

I also found the efficiency claims somewhat hard to interpret. RealMotion offline is reported at 62 ms versus QCNet at 94 ms, but RealMotion online is 20 ms and offline requires “three times latency” because only the final prediction is used for evaluation. This suggests the benchmark comparison may effectively amortize multiple sequential calls into one final score, which again differs from standard one-shot evaluation. The paper should make explicit whether the reported leaderboard submission used the offline or online mode, and exactly what input sequence was available at each prediction time. If the online mode is the intended deployment setting, then the most relevant comparison would be against online-capable baselines under the same repeated-inference protocol.

The writing quality is below the standard expected for a top-tier conference. There are many grammatical errors, awkward phrasings, and notation inconsistencies. Some equations are poorly formatted or incomplete; Equation (4) in particular appears malformed in the provided text. Several terms are introduced informally or inconsistently, such as “interested agents” versus “agents of interest,” “temporarly relaying,” and “one’s” instead of “ones.” These issues do not invalidate the ideas, but they make the paper harder to evaluate and reproduce. The methodology section would benefit from a clearer algorithmic description of training and inference, including pseudocode for the recurrent rollout over sub-scenes and memory updates.

Despite these weaknesses, I think the paper has real merit. The problem framing is timely, the proposed temporal reuse of scene context and prior predictions is sensible, and the empirical gains are large enough that they are unlikely to be entirely accidental. I especially like that the paper tries to bridge benchmark practice and deployment reality rather than only optimizing one-shot metrics. The main question for acceptance is whether the current evidence is sufficient to support the stronger claims of state of the art and practical superiority. In my view, the answer is not yet fully yes, because the comparisons are not sufficiently controlled and the continuous-setting reformulation is not evaluated against appropriately adapted baselines.

To strengthen the paper, I would strongly recommend the following. First, move a matched-baseline study into the main paper: train at least one strong prior model, ideally QCNet, on the reorganized continuous data and compare against RealMotion under the same protocol. Second, clarify the exact evaluation setup and explicitly distinguish standard benchmark performance from continuous-setting performance. Third, provide more details on the recurrence, memory bank maintenance, and identity association assumptions. Fourth, add scenario-wise analysis showing where temporal continuity helps most. Fifth, improve the writing and fix notation/equation issues.

My overall assessment is moderately positive on the idea and empirical promise, but tempered by concerns about fairness and clarity. I would lean toward acceptance if the conference values practical reframing and strong empirical results, but I also think the paper needs revision to meet the standard of methodological rigor expected at top venues.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes RealMotion, a motion forecasting framework for continuous driving that departs from the standard independent-scene formulation. The method reorganizes existing forecasting datasets into temporally ordered sub-scenes, then applies two recurrent temporal modules: a scene context stream that propagates historical scene features via cross-attention after coordinate alignment, and an agent trajectory stream that refines current predictions using a memory bank of past predicted trajectories and mode features. Experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2, including single-agent and multi-agent settings, report strong leaderboard performance and favorable latency/parameter trade-offs relative to several baselines.
strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant mismatch between benchmark evaluation and real deployment, namely repeated forecasting over continuous driving rather than isolated scenes.
The proposed framework is conceptually intuitive: separating temporal scene-context accumulation from trajectory-level refinement is a reasonable design that aligns with the problem structure.
Empirical results are strong on Argoverse 2 leaderboard metrics and competitive on Argoverse 1, with clear gains over the paper's independent variant.
Includes ablations on major components such as data reorganization, scene-context stream, trajectory stream, alignment modules, trajectory embedding, and attention depth.
Efficiency analysis suggests the model is relatively lightweight in parameter count and online latency compared with some strong baselines.
weaknesses: The central experimental claim is weakened by a potentially unfair comparison: RealMotion uses a different problem setup via data reorganization and sequential inference, while most baselines are reported from standard benchmark settings without analogous continuous-context adaptation.

The paper does not clearly establish whether gains come primarily from the new architecture or from exposing the model to additional effective context through the reorganized data and repeated refinement steps.
Method description lacks precision in several places, with ambiguous notation and incomplete definitions for key operations, making reproduction difficult.
The trajectory-memory mechanism relies on past predicted trajectories, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze error accumulation, drift, or robustness when earlier predictions are poor.

Claims about real-world efficiency are only partially substantiated because offline evaluation uses three passes while online latency is reported separately without a standardized end-to-end comparison against similarly cached/adapted baselines.

Novelty relative to prior temporal/streaming forecasting ideas is moderate; the paper positions itself against isolated-scene methods, but related streaming work is only briefly discussed and not deeply compared.
methodological_flaws: There is a scientific validity concern in comparing RealMotion leaderboard results against prior methods trained/evaluated under the standard independent-scene benchmark protocol. Because the paper changes the effective input structure through retrospective scene serialization, the comparison may not isolate model quality from task reformulation.

The data reorganization strategy may introduce information leakage or altered supervision semantics if sub-scenes are retrospectively constructed from a full original sample. The paper states that split points are chosen along historical frames and future segments are extended using available ground truth, but it does not rigorously clarify what information is available at each sub-scene during training and evaluation, nor whether map/agent aggregation across split points preserves strict causality.

Equation (1) does not actually define a geometric projection from the previous local coordinate system to the current one; applying Motion-aware LayerNorm conditioned on relative pose is not equivalent to coordinate transformation. Thus the claim that features are 'projected' or 'aligned' is mathematically imprecise.

Equation (3) for trajectory alignment is under-specified and appears dimensionally inconsistent or incomplete. The transformation uses only a rotation matrix and subtraction of an origin point indexed by Δt·q, but translation into the current frame and heading-difference handling are not rigorously defined. It is unclear whether θ is absolute heading or relative heading, and whether the transpose yields the intended K×2 output.

The loss definition contains an apparent typo/inconsistency: the text introduces L_refine but Eq. (5) uses L_refin. More importantly, equal weighting of regression, classification, and refinement losses is asserted without justification or sensitivity analysis.

Empirical validity is limited by the absence of controlled baseline adaptations. A stronger test would compare against strong baselines retrained on the same reorganized continuous data and/or equipped with comparable recurrent memory. The appendix mention of QCNet adaptation is not included in the main evidence.

The paper claims lower real-world inference latency, but the reported offline numbers are not directly comparable to standard one-shot benchmark inference, and the online numbers omit accuracy under the same online protocol for competing methods except HPTR. This weakens the causal link between the proposed design and deployment efficiency.

No statistical significance, variance across runs, or robustness analysis is provided, despite many ablation gains being modest (e.g., alignment and TE improvements). This makes it hard to judge whether some reported improvements are stable.
